**[p. 25] Sūrat al-Fātiḥah**

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

It is Makkan, and it is said to be Madinan. The more correct view is that it is both Makkan and Madinan. It was revealed in Makkah when the prayer (ṣalāh) was made obligatory, and then it was revealed again in Madinah when the qiblah was changed to the Ka'bah. It is called Umm al-Qur'ān (the Mother of the Qur'an) because of a ḥadīth, and because it includes the meanings found in the Qur'an. It is also called Sūrat al-Wāfiyah and al-Kāfiyah for this reason, and Sūrat al-Kanz (the Treasure), based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying, relating from Allah the Exalted: "The Opening of the Book is a treasure from the treasures of My Throne." It is called Sūrat al-Shifā' and al-Shāfiyah, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The Opening of the Book is a cure for every disease except death (sām)." It is called Sūrat al-Mathānī, because it is recited twice in every prayer. It is called Sūrat al-Ṣalāh (the Surah of the Prayer), because of what is related, and because it is either obligatory (wājib) or an obligation (farīḍah) in prayer. It is called Sūrat al-Ḥamd (the Surah of Praise) and al-Asās (the Foundation), for it is the foundation of the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "If you become ill or suffer an ailment, then hold to al-Asās." Its number of verses is seven by agreement. And Allah knows best.

﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾

The reciters of Madinah, Basrah and Syria hold that the basmalah is not a verse of al-Fātiḥah, nor of any other surah. It was written only to separate surahs and to seek blessing by beginning with it. This is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah and those who follow him (may Allah have mercy on them), and for this reason they do not recite it aloud in the prayer. The reciters of Makkah and Kufah hold that it is a verse of al-Fātiḥah and of every surah. Al-Shāfi'ī and his companions (may Allah have mercy on them) follow this view, and for this reason they recite it aloud. They say: "The early generation (al-salaf) wrote it in the muṣḥaf, along with the command to keep the Qur'an free of what is not part of it." It is reported from Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with them both): "Whoever leaves it out has left out one hundred and fourteen verses of the Book of Allah."

Our proof is the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah, who said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Allah the Exalted said: I have divided the prayer (ṣalāh), meaning al-Fātiḥah, between Me and My servant into two halves, and My servant shall have what he asks. When the servant says: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, Allah the Exalted says: My servant has praised Me. When he says: ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, Allah the Exalted says: My servant has extolled Me. When he says: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾, He says: My servant has glorified Me. When he says: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, He says: This is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks. When he says: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those You have blessed, not of those who have incurred wrath, nor of those who are astray﴾, He says: This is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks."

The beginning with ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ is evidence that the basmalah is not part of al-Fātiḥah. If it is not part of al-Fātiḥah, it is by consensus not part of any other surah. The ḥadīth is recorded in Ṣiḥāḥ al-Maṣābīḥ. What they cite does not harm our position, because the basmalah is a verse of the Qur'an revealed for separation and for seeking blessing in beginning with it between surahs, according to us. Fakhr al-Islām mentioned this in al-Mabsūṭ. The objection to us would only apply if we did not regard it as a verse of the Qur'an. The full explanation is in al-Kāfī.

The letter bā' (in bi-smi) is connected to an omitted verb whose estimated form is: "In the name of Allah I read" or "I recite," because the one who recites the basmalah is reading. Similarly, when a traveller stops and departs and says: "In the name of Allah and blessings," the meaning is: "In the name of Allah I alight," and "In the name of Allah I depart." Likewise the one who slaughters, and every doer who begins his act with "In the name of Allah," has an implied verb that makes the basmalah his starting point. The omitted verb is estimated as delayed (muta'akhkhiran) because what matters more is the verb together with what is connected to it, [and that is what is connected to it]. The pagans used to begin with the names of their gods, saying: "In the name of al-Lāt," and "In the name of al-'Uzzā." So it is required that the monotheist intend the meaning of singling out the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for the beginning. This is achieved by placing it first and delaying the verb. The verb is placed first in ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1] because it is, according to one view, the first surah revealed, and the command to read was more important. So placing the verb first was more fitting. It is also possible to take "iqra'" (read) as meaning: "Perform the recitation and carry it out," like the saying: "So-and-so gives and withholds," where the verb is not transitive to a specific object. And "bi-smi rabbika" could be the object of the following "iqra'." The name of Allah is connected to the recitation in the way that oil is connected to growth in the verse ﴿a tree that grows with oil﴾ [al-Mu'minūn: 20]. The meaning is: "Seeking blessing through the name of Allah, read." In this there is instruction to His servants on how to seek blessing through His name, and how to honour it.

The bā' is built on kasrah (vowel "i"), because it always accompanies a noun and the genitive (jarr), so it takes a kasrah so that its vowel resembles its function. The word ism (name) is among those nouns whose initial letters were built on sukūn (silence), like ibn (son) and ibnah (daughter) and others. When they pronounce them at the start of speech, they add a hamzah to avoid beginning with a silent letter. When it occurs in continuous speech (al-darj), there is no need to add anything. Some do not add it and dispense with it by vowelling the silent letter, and they say: sam and sum. It is one of the nouns whose final parts are omitted, like yad (hand) and dam (blood). Its original form is sumuww, as evidenced by its inflection like asmā', sammā, sammat. Its derivation is from al-sumuww, which means elevation, because naming (tasmiyah) raises the named and proclaims mention of it.

The alif is omitted in writing here, but it is kept in His saying ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1], because in that case the alif is written even though it is dropped in pronunciation due to frequent use. The bā' is lengthened as a substitute for the omitted alif. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Azīz said to his scribe: "Lengthen the bā', make the sīns clear, and round the mīm."

**Allāh**: its original form is al-Ilāh. Its parallel is al-Nās (the people), whose original form is al-Unās. The hamzah was dropped and the definite article was substituted for it. Al-Ilāh is a common noun (ism jins), applied to every object of worship, whether true or false. Then it became specific to the object of worship in truth, just as al-Najm (the star) was a name for every star and then became specific to the Pleiades (al-Thurayyā). As for Allāh with the hamzah dropped, it is specific to the Truth and is not applied to anyone else. It is a proper noun (ism ghayr ṣifah), because you describe it but do not use it as a descriptor. You do not say "a thing is Ilāh," just as you do not say "a thing is a man." You say: "Ilāh wāḥid ṣamad" (one God, eternal refuge). Also, the attributes of Allah the Exalted must have a subject to which they apply. If you made all of them attributes, they would remain attributes not applied to a named subject, and that is not permissible. This name has no derivation according to al-Khalīl, al-Zajjāj, Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl. It is said that derivation means that two or more forms share one meaning. The form of this name and the form of their saying alaha (to be bewildered) share the meaning of bewilderment and perplexity, because human imaginings are bewildered in knowing the object of worship and confound the intelligent. For this reason error is widespread, falsehood spreads, and correct reflection is rare. It is also said that it is derived from their saying alaha ya'lahu ilāhan, meaning "he was worshipped," so it is a verbal noun in the sense of ma'lūh, that is, "worshipped," like His saying ﴿This is the creation of Allah﴾ [Luqmān: 11], meaning "His creation." Its lām is emphasised (tufakhkhamu) when it is preceded by a fatḥah or ḍammah, and made thin (turaqqaqu) when preceded by a kasrah. Some make it thin in every case and some emphasise it in every case, but the majority follow the first rule.

**al-Raḥmān**: the form fa'lān from raḥima (to show mercy), meaning the one whose mercy encompasses everything, like ghaḍbān from ghaḍiba (to be angry), meaning one who is full of anger. Likewise **al-Raḥīm** is fa'īl from it, like marīḍ from maraḍa (to be ill). Al-Raḥmān has more intensity than al-Raḥīm, because al-Raḥīm has one extra letter while al-Raḥmān has two extra letters, and increase in the wording indicates increase in meaning. For this reason it is said in supplication: "O Raḥmān of this world," because it includes both the believer and the unbeliever, "and Raḥīm of the Hereafter," because it is specific to the believer. They say: al-Raḥmān is specific as a name, because no one else is described by it, and general in meaning, for the reason we have explained. Al-Raḥīm is the reverse, because it is applied to others too, and it is specific to the believers. For this reason He put al-Raḥmān first, even though it is more intense. The rule is ascent from lower to higher, as one says: "So-and-so is a learned, skilled scholar." This is because al-Raḥmān is like a proper name for what no one other than Allah is described by. The mercy of Allah is His bestowal of favour upon His servants, and its origin is tenderness (al-'aṭf). As for the poet's verse about Musaylimah:

"You are the rain of the people; may you never cease to be al-Raḥmān."

that is a form of their obstinacy in disbelief.

The word Raḥmān is not diptote (ghayr munṣarif) according to the one who holds that the condition is the absence of the feminine fa'lānah, since it has no feminine fa'lānah. According to the one who holds that the condition is the presence of fa'lā, he makes it diptote, since it has no fa'lā. The first view is the correct one.

**﴿Al-ḥamd﴾** (praise) is the attribution of beauty to something on the basis of excellence. It is in the nominative case as the *mubtada'* (subject of the nominal sentence), though its original form is the accusative. It has been read with its verb expressed, on the basis that it is one of the verbal nouns (*maṣādir*) put in the accusative with an implied verb, in the sense of informing, like the saying "shukran" (thanks) and "kufran" (ingratitude). The shift from the accusative to the nominative indicates the permanence and stability of the meaning. The predicate (*khabar*) is **﴿lillāh﴾** (to God). The *lām* is connected to an omitted element, meaning "obligatory" or "established."

It has been said: *ḥamd* and *madḥ* (praise) are brothers, and both mean commendation and proclaiming the beauty of something, whether a blessing or otherwise. You say: "I praised the man for his generosity (*ḥamadtu al-rajul ʿalā inʿāmihi*), and I praised him for his courage and noble lineage." As for *shukr* (gratitude), it is specifically for a blessing, and it is by the heart, the tongue and the limbs. The poet said:

"The bounty has conferred upon you three things from me: my hand, my tongue, and the hidden heart."

"*Ḥamd*" is by the tongue alone, and it is one of the branches of gratitude. From it is the hadith: "Praise is the head of gratitude; no servant thanks God who does not praise Him." He made it the head of gratitude because mentioning a blessing by the tongue spreads it more than belief and the conduct of the limbs, because the work of the heart is hidden, and because of the possibility of error in the work of the limbs. The opposite of *ḥamd* is blame (*dhamm*), and the opposite of *shukr* is ingratitude (*kufrān*).

It has been said: *madḥ* is praise for what is possessed of the attributes of perfection, such as His being everlasting, capable, knowing, eternal and without beginning. *Shukr* is praise for what comes from Him of the attributes of bounty, and *ḥamd* encompasses both.

The *alif* and *lām* in it indicate comprehensiveness (*istighrāq*) according to us, unlike the **Muʿtazilah**. For this reason it is joined with the name of God (p-30), because it is a name of the essence, which gathers all the attributes of perfection. This is a building upon the question of the creation of actions, and I have verified it in several places.

**﴿Rabbi al-ʿālamīn﴾** (Lord of the worlds). *Al-Rabb* means the owner. From it is the saying of Ṣafwān to Abū Sufyān: "That a man of Quraysh should be my *rabb* is dearer to me than that a man of Hawāzin should be my *rabb*." You say: "*rabbahu yarubbuhu*, so he is a *rabb*." It is permissible that it be a description by the verbal noun for emphasis, as "justice" (*ʿadl*) is used as a description. The word *rabb* is only used absolutely for God alone, but among slaves it is used with a qualifier: **﴿Innahu rabbī aḥsana mathwāya﴾** (Indeed, He is my Lord; He has made my residence good) [Yūsuf: 23], and **﴿Irjiʿ ilā rabbika﴾** (Return to your lord) [Yūsuf: 50].

Al-Wāsiṭī said: He is the Creator from the beginning, the Nourisher in sustenance, and the Forgiver at the end, and He is the Greatest Name of God.

*Al-ʿālam* (the world) is what the Creator is known by among bodies, substances and accidents, or it is every existent other than God Most High. It was so named because it is a sign (*ʿalam*) of His existence. It has been pluralized with the *wāw* and *nūn* (ending *-īn*), although it is specific to the attributes of rational beings, or what is in their category of markers, because it contains the meaning of description, and that is: indicating the meaning of knowledge.

Qur'an 1:3: ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. Their mention has already passed, and it is evidence that the basmala (the formula "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful") is not part of al-Fatiha, for if it were part of it, He would not have repeated them, since repetition without benefit is empty of meaning.

﴿Mālik﴾ (Master/Owner): ʿĀṣim and ʿAlī read it as (مَلِكِ, *Malik*, King). Others read it differently. This is the preferred reading according to some scholars, because (the word) does not require an annexed complement (*iḍāfa*, genitive construction), and because of His saying: ﴿Whose is the dominion today?﴾ [Ghāfir 40:16]. Also, every king is an owner, but not every owner is a king. Further, the command of a king is carried out over an owner, but not the reverse. It has also been said that *mālik* carries greater reward, because it has more letters. Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Ḥasan, may God be pleased with them both, read (مَلَكَ, *Malaka*).

﴿Yawm al-Dīn﴾ (the Day of Judgement), meaning the Day of Recompense. It is said: "As you judge, so you will be judged," meaning, as you act, so you will be repaid. This is an *idāfa* of an active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*) to a time expression by way of extension (*ittisāʿ*), like the saying of the Arabs: "O thief of the night, (you are) the people of the house," meaning: the Owner of all affairs on the Day of Religion. The specification with the Day of Religion is because the command on that Day belongs to God alone. Its being a descriptor of a definite noun was permitted even though the *idāfa* of an active participle is not a true (strictly definite) *idāfa*, because it is intended to express continuity, so the *idāfa* became a true one, and it was therefore permissible for it to be a descriptor of a definite noun.

These attributes applied to God, glory be to Him, namely that He is Lord, i.e., Owner of all the worlds, Bestower of all blessings, and Owner of all affairs on the Day of Reward and Punishment, come after the indication of the exclusivity of praise to Him in His saying: ﴿All praise belongs to God﴾. This is evidence that whoever has these attributes is more deserving of praise and commendation than anyone else.

The commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 1, verse 5:

﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.﴾ *Iyya* (إيّا), according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, is a pronoun (*ism mudmar*). According to Sibawayh, the *kaf* (الكاف) is a particle of address (*harf khitab*) with no place in *i'rab* (grammatical case-inflection). According to al-Khalil, it is a pronoun, and *iyya* is annexed to it, because it resembles a noun, since it precedes the verb and the subject. The Kufans said: *iyyaka* in its entirety is a noun. The fronting of the object is for the purpose of exclusivity (*ikhtisas*), and the meaning is: we single You out for worship, which is the utmost degree of submission and humility, and we single You out for seeking help. He shifted from the third person (*ghayba*) to the second person (*khitab*) for *iltifat* (the shift of grammatical person within discourse). This may occur from the third person to the second, from the second to the third, or from the third to the first person, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until when you are in the ship and they sail with them by a good wind﴾ [Yunus: 22], and His saying: ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds, and We drive them﴾ [Fatir: 9], and the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*Your night has stretched long at al-Ithmid, and the free-hearted one slept while you did not sleep.*

*He spent the night, and his night spent the night with him, like the night of one with a sore, inflamed eye.*

*That is a report that came to me, and I was informed of it concerning Abu al-Aswad.*

In the three verses he shifted, for he did not say: "your night" (*layli*), "I spent the night" (*bittu*), "came to you" (*ja'aki*). The Arabs use this a great deal, and they consider that when speech moves from one style to another, it is more readily accepted by the listener, better refreshes his energy, and fills his attentiveness with anticipation. Its positions may be specialized with benefits and subtleties which are rarely made clear except to the skilled experts and the learned masters of the field, and they are few. Among what is distinctive about this position is that when He mentioned the One deserving of praise and commendation (*al-Haqq bi'l-hamd wa'l-thana'*), and attributed to Him those great attributes, knowledge became attached to a known object of great importance, deserving of praise, of utmost submission, and of seeking help in matters of importance. So that known object, distinguished by those attributes, was addressed, and it was said: "You alone, O One whose attributes are these, we worship and we ask for help, not any other than You." The worship was placed before the seeking of help, because placing the means before the request for a need is closer to being answered; or for the sake of the arrangement of the verses, just as He placed *al-Rahman* first, although the more eloquent form is not to be placed first. The seeking of help is stated without restriction so that it encompasses every matter in which help is sought. It is also possible that what is meant is seeking help through Him and through His granting success in performing the worship, and His saying: ﴿Guide us﴾ serves as an explanation of what is sought of the help, as if it were said: "How shall I help you?" So they said:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 1, verse 6:

﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾. That is: keep us firm upon the clear method, like your saying to one who is standing: "Stand (qum) until I return to you," meaning: remain in the state you are in. Or: guide us in the future as You have guided us in the present. Hada (to guide) is transitive to one object directly; as for its being transitive to another object, it has come transitive to it directly, as in this verse, and it has come transitive with the preposition lam and with ila, as in His exalted saying: ﴿He guided us to this﴾ [al-A'raf: 43], and His saying: ﴿My Lord has guided me to a straight path﴾ [al-An'am: 161]. Al-sirat (the path) means the main road, from saraṭa al-shay' (he swallowed the thing), as if it swallows up the travellers when they take it. Al-sirat is derived from the substitution of the sin with a sad, due to the affinity of the ta' in emphasis (itbaq), because the sad, the dad, the ta' and the za' are among the emphatic letters (huruf al-itbaq). The sad may be mixed with the sound of the zay, because the zay is closer to the ta', as both are voiced (majhurah). This is the recitation of Hamzah. The sin is the recitation of Ibn Kathir throughout the Qur'an, and it is the original form of the word. The rest read with a pure sad, and it is the dialect of Quraysh, and it is the one established in the Imam (the standard codex). It may be masculine or feminine, like al-tariq and al-sabil. What is meant by it is the path of truth, which is the religion of Islam.

(p-33) ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the path," and it is in the position of repeating the governing element (al-'amil). Its benefit is emphasis and the indication that the straight path is explained as the path of the Muslims, so that this serves as a testimony to the path of the Muslims being upright in the most eloquent and most emphatic manner. They are the believers, or the prophets (peace be upon them), or the people of Musa before they changed.

﴿Not of those who have incurred anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ is a substitute for "those upon whom You have bestowed favour," meaning: those upon whom favour has been bestowed are those who were safe from the anger of Allah and from misguidance. Or it is an attribute (sifah) of "those" (alladhina), meaning: they combined absolute favour, which is the favour of faith, with safety from the anger of Allah and from misguidance. The occurrence of this as an attribute of "those," although "those" is definite and ghayr (not) is not made definite by being annexed, is permissible because when it falls between two opposites that are both definite, it becomes definite through annexation, as in: "I was amazed by the movement not of the stillness" (ʿajibtu min al-ḥarakati ghayri al-sukūni). "Those upon whom favour has been bestowed" and "those upon whom anger has been incurred" are opposites. Also, alladhina is close to an indefinite (nakirah), since no specific people are intended by it, while ghayri al-maghdubi ʿalayhim is close to a definite, because of the specification it obtains through its annexation. So each of the two has ambiguity in one respect and specificity in another, and so they are equal. As for ʿalayhim, the first (ʿalayhim) has its place in the accusative as object (maf'ul), and the second (ʿalayhim) has its place in the nominative as subject (fa'il). The anger of Allah is the will to take vengeance upon the deniers, and the sending down of punishment upon them, and that He does to them what a king does when he is angry at those under his hand. It is said: those upon whom anger has been incurred are the Jews, due to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whom Allah has cursed and upon whom He has become angry﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60]. And those who are astray are the Christians, due to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They have certainly gone astray before﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 77]. And "la" (not) is an extra particle according to the Basrans, for emphasis, and according to the Kufans it is in the sense of ghayr (other than).

"Amin": a sound (sawt) named as the verb which is istajib (answer/grant), just as ruwayda is a noun for amhil (give respite). And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the meaning of 'Amin,' and he said: 'Do it.'" It is indeclinable (mabni), and in it there are two dialects: lengthening its alif and shortening it, and the shortened form is the original; the lengthening is with the hamzah fully articulated. He said:

Allah has mercy upon a servant who says "Amin"

And he said:

"Amin," so Allah increased what is between us of distance

He ﷺ said: "Jibril taught me 'Amin' at the recitation of the Opening of the Book, and said: indeed it is like the seal upon the book." And it is not from the Qur'an, as evidenced by the fact that it is not established in the mushafs.
